title: 30 Solo Date Ideas You'll Actually Want to Take Yourself On, and the Little Kit for Each
dek: Thirty solo dates for every mood: a sketch outing, a film walk, a picnic for one, each with the small thing worth bringing. Table for one, and a very good table at that.

body.text: A solo date is time you've decided to spend well, with the one person whose taste you already know. No negotiating over dinner, no checking whether anyone's bored, no leaving early because someone else is tired.

Below are thirty ideas for getting out of the house, starting with the dates where one small thing in your bag (a pocket watercolor set, a film camera, a good pair of walking shoes) makes the hour easier and prettier, and ending with free ways to start and a few places to go. Staying in is a different list: [20 cozy solo date ideas you can do at home](/journal/cozy-solo-dates-at-home). Pick one, put it in the calendar and go.
Why it feels odd (and why that fades)

Most of the discomfort is an imagined audience: you picture a room full of people noticing you're alone, while they're looking at their own plate, phone or conversation. Three small habits help. Bring something for your hands, like a book, a notebook or a sketchbook. Choose a spot with a natural place for one, like a counter or a window ledge. And decide in advance how long you're staying, so there's an end in sight.

items: **First time out alone:** the coffee shop and a chapter (15) or a pocket watercolor outing (1). Both are short and easy to leave.
**Only an hour free:** a sketch of a cafe corner (2), a fresh-flower stop (17) or a thrift hunt (16).
**Want something to show for it:** the film walk (3), the junk-journal page (4) or the pocket watercolor outing (1).
**Need to be outside:** the birdwatching bench (8), a picnic for one (9) or a lakeside sit (14).
**Feeling brave:** the museum visit (6) or the short beginner hike (7).

body.title: Pocket-sized watercolor outing
body.note: A small travel set, a cup of water and a bench. Paint one view in three colors and call it finished. The [watercolor](/journal/watercolor-painting-for-beginners) guide has the first techniques. **What makes it easier:** a pocket watercolor set with a built-in palette and a small sketch pad, so one view fits in a coat pocket.
body.first: Pick the view before you unpack, then paint it in three colors and stop.

body.title: Sketch a cafe corner
body.note: Draw the lamp, the mugs, the curve of a chair. Looking closely is the point, not accuracy. **What makes it easier:** a small sketch pad and {{product:sakura-pigma-micron-8-pack-black|a fine black pen}}, so an outline of the lamp or the mugs is ready in a minute.
body.first: Pick one object on your table and draw only its outline for fifteen minutes.

body.title: Single-roll film walk
body.note: A film camera slows you down, because every frame counts. Plan a route and choose each shot. **What makes it easier:** a reusable film camera, so every frame feels chosen and the roll becomes a keepsake.

body.title: Junk journal your week
body.note: Collect a ticket, a receipt and a wrapper and glue them into a notebook with one sentence per day. [Here's how](/journal/how-to-start-junk-journaling). **What makes it easier:** {{product:stationery-island-a5-blank-journal-180-pages|a thick-paged notebook}} and a few rolls of {{product:mr-pen-washi-tape-21-rolls|washi tape}}, so the week's ticket and receipt become a page.

body.title: A short story over lunch
body.note: Set a timer for twenty minutes and write about the stranger at the next table. Change everything about them. **What makes it easier:** a pocket notebook, so the first sentence about the stranger gets written down before it fades.
body.first: Write the first sentence about someone you can see, then change their name, job and destination.

body.title: Museum visit, reader's-eye edition
body.note: Choose one artwork and write three sentences about what's happening in it. Then read the label and compare notes. **What makes it easier:** a slim notebook that fits in a coat pocket, for your three sentences and the label notes.
body.first: Pick a room near the entrance and sit with a single piece for ten minutes before you write anything.

body.title: For a make-something date
body.dek: A pocket watercolor set, a sketch pad, a film camera, a thick-paged journal or a notebook that fits in a coat pocket: each makes a date out easier and prettier. Pick the one that matches the date you're dreaming up.

body.title: Short beginner hike
body.note: Choose a well-marked, popular trail in daylight, check the weather, carry water and tell someone your route and when you'll be back. Park services advise against hiking alone, so bring a friend if you can. **Worth bringing:** walking shoes with some grip, trekking-style socks, a small daypack and a water bottle, so water and a snack ride on your back; a phone armband keeps a map or music in reach.

body.title: Birdwatching bench
body.note: Sit still for twenty minutes and list every bird you notice, named or not. Describe the color and the song. **Worth bringing:** compact binoculars, which bring a distant branch close enough to see the colors, and a pocket notebook for the list.

body.title: Picnic for one
body.note: A sandwich, a piece of fruit, something sweet. [The picnic guide](/journal/how-to-plan-a-perfect-picnic) has the checklist. **What makes it easier:** a picnic blanket and a small insulated bag or flask, so lunch has a spot to land.

body.title: Stargazing night
body.note: Find an open space that is easy to reach, bring a blanket and something warm to drink, and give your eyes time to adjust. Tell someone where you're going and plan how you'll get home. **Worth bringing:** a picnic blanket and a thermos flask, so you can sit comfortably while your eyes adjust.

body.title: Roller-skating session
body.note: Rinks and smooth paved paths are a friendly place to start, and wobbling is part of it. Wear a helmet, wrist guards and knee and elbow pads, and skate in daylight. **What makes it easier:** a set of skate protective gear, so the helmet, wrist guards and pads above are ready in one bag.

body.title: Bike ride with a destination
body.note: Pick a path or park trail that ends somewhere nice: a lake, a lookout, a bakery. **What makes it easier:** a small daypack and a water bottle, so a snack and a layer ride on your back.

body.title: Rainy-day walk
body.note: Wet streets, reflections, a podcast and a decent umbrella. Pack dry socks for the end. **Worth bringing:** walking shoes and a spare pair of dry trekking-style socks in your bag, so wet streets stay fun right to the end.

body.title: Beach or lakeside sit
body.note: Bring a book you really want to read and a hat. Keep the phone in your bag for the first half hour. **Worth bringing:** a picnic blanket and a book sleeve, so the paperback survives the bag and you have a spot to settle.

body.title: For a date outdoors
body.dek: Walking shoes, trekking-style socks, a small daypack and a bottle, plus a phone armband for the map or the music and binoculars for the bench.

body.title: Coffee shop and a chapter
body.note: Order something you wouldn't make at home, take the window seat and read one chapter before you touch your phone. The full walk-through is in [how to take yourself on a solo coffee shop date](/journal/how-to-take-yourself-on-a-solo-coffee-shop-date). **What makes it easier:** a book sleeve and a pocket notebook, so a paperback and a page of thoughts fit in one tote.

body.title: Thrift store treasure hunt
body.note: Give yourself a small budget and a mission: a mug, a scarf, a frame. Leave when the money or the hour runs out. **Worth bringing:** a roomy market tote, so the mug, scarf and frame get home in one piece.
body.first: Pick the mission before you walk in, and only pick up what you can picture on your own shelf.

body.title: A fresh-flower stop
body.note: Buy a small bunch, plonk it in whatever vessel you have and put it where you'll see it first thing tomorrow. **What makes it easier:** a small vase and a pair of flower snips, so the bunch looks arranged by tomorrow morning.

body.title: For the picnic, the rink and the treat
body.dek: A blanket and a flask for the park, protective gear for the rink, a market tote and a small vase for the treats you carry home.

body.text: How to eat alone and enjoy it
Eating alone is the part people dread most, and it's mostly a logistics problem.

items: **Choose the seat, not just the restaurant.** Counter, bar-style and window seats are built for one, and many places have them, so ask when you arrive.
**Go off-peak.** An early lunch or mid-afternoon bite is quieter, and staff have time to be friendly.
**Bring a prop.** A book or sketchbook gives you somewhere to look and something to do while you wait.
**Order the thing you'd normally share.** The whole point of going alone is that the dessert is entirely yours.
**Keep your phone in your bag until the food arrives.** Then see if you still want it.

body.text: Pick well-lit, busy places, especially after dark, and go with someone when you can. Tell someone where you're going and when you'll be home. Two personal tips, not official advice: share your location with a friend if you're comfortable doing so, and keep your phone charged. If a place or situation feels off, leave. You never owe anyone an explanation, and a good solo date is one where you feel at ease.
Eight ways in that need nothing but a free hour.

body.title: Library wander
body.note: Give yourself twenty minutes in a section you never visit, then borrow one book purely because of the cover or the first line. **Worth bringing:** a book sleeve, so the borrowed book rides safely in your bag.

body.title: Golden-hour walk with a theme
body.note: Choose a theme like doors, blue things or cats in windows, and find ten examples before you head home. **Worth bringing:** comfortable walking shoes and a phone armband, so ten photos and a playlist stay within reach.

body.title: Park-bench people-watching
body.note: Jot down five anonymous details in a notebook: a dog's outfit, someone's excellent coat, the ice cream truck's jingle. No names, no staring. **Worth bringing:** a pocket notebook for the five details.

body.title: Sunrise or sunset spot
body.note: Find a hill, waterfront or open public space and arrive ten minutes early. **Worth bringing:** a thermos flask, so the warm drink is still warm when the sky changes.

body.title: Neighborhood detail crawl
body.note: Pick a street and photograph one detail per block: a doorknob, a tile pattern, a fire escape. **What makes it easier:** a reusable film camera, so one frame per block makes a tidy little set.

body.title: A museum or gallery hour
body.note: Some museums have free or pay-what-you-can hours, and some small galleries are free, so check locally. Choose one room and stay with it.

body.title: Bookstore browse
body.note: Read the first page of five books you'd never normally pick up, and note the one you'd go back for.

body.title: A postcard to future you
body.note: Tell yourself what you're up to today and what you're hoping for in six months. Post it on the way home. **Worth bringing:** a small letter-writing set with a few cards and envelopes, so the postcard is ready to post on the way home.

body.title: Matinee movie
body.note: Some cinemas have cheaper daytime or weekday tickets, so check yours. Sit in the middle and bring the snack you actually want.

body.title: Farmers' market breakfast
body.note: Wander the stalls first, then buy a pastry and something seasonal. Eat on a bench. **Worth bringing:** a market tote for the seasonal haul.

body.title: Dessert-only dinner
body.note: Skip the main course and go straight to the good part. Take the counter seat if there is one.

body.title: Pottery-painting walk-in
body.note: Studios where you paint a ready-made piece can suit solo visitors, though walk-in policies and prices vary, so check first. Prefer to make your own at home? Try [air-dry clay](/journal/how-to-start-air-dry-clay).

body.title: Paddle or boat rental
body.note: Some waterfronts rent kayaks, canoes or pedal boats by the hour. Check local rules and the weather first, and wear a life jacket.

body.text: Want a whole day built around one of these? Try [how to plan a solo Saturday](/journal/how-to-plan-a-solo-saturday), or let [Make Some Plans](/make-plans) match an idea to your energy, budget and free hours.
